source.title: DBAT: Dynamic Backward Attention Transformer for Material Segmentation with Cross-Resolution Patches
source.authors: Yuwen Heng; S. Dasmahapatra; Hansung Kim

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses mixed or uninterpretable neuron features and reports network-dissection concept alignments, but it does not test whether individual neurons respond strongly to several unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The network-dissection results count neurons aligned with semantic concepts; they do not directly measure multiple unrelated inputs activating the same neuron. The paper's statements that some remaining neurons may detect mixed features are explanatory, not a reported test of that behavior. Segmentation-performance and attention results do not measure the claim. Results cited from other work were not included.
record.test_reason: A material-segmentation paper whose network dissection counts last-layer neurons whose top-0.5% activation masks best match one Broden concept (IoU>0.04). It does not measure whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. Its remark that unaligned neurons may detect mixed features (texture plus object) is an untested explanation. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude DBAT is the most accurate of the real-time models compared (86.85% Pixel Acc on LMD). They also conclude it uses cross-resolution patch features (about half the information from small patches) and is especially good at texture features. They say pre-trained object detectors ease training of texture detectors, and that networks differ in the features they learn. They note dissection interprets only disentangled neurons, and call for densely labelled material datasets.
record.recipe_differences: Uses network dissection to align neurons with semantic labels; it does not apply the cited original-source method for testing polysemantic neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported semantic concept alignments vary with pre-training, task, and network architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: The share of last-layer neurons aligned to each Broden concept (colour, texture, part, object, scene) differs by task, pre-training and architecture. EfficientNet-b5 has almost no texture-aligned neurons on either task. Values are shown only in figures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision models, the concepts that disentangled last-layer neurons align with depend on the training task, pre-training and architecture.

record.problems: The network-dissection analysis only interprets neurons aligned to semantic concepts, uses the last encoder layer, and does not directly test whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. The concept-alignment values appear in figures and are not numerically stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Segmentation accuracy, attention-weight, and CKA results were left out because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity. No other directly relevant results were omitted.

untested.parts: Whether individual neurons in vision models respond to several unrelated inputs. Dissection assigns only one best label per neuron, and the unaligned share is not analysed.
Superposition or capacity as the cause is not examined.
Causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure are not examined.
Concept-alignment profiles differ by architecture and pre-training. The polysemantic share and its performance cost are not measured.
Whether apparent polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature is not examined.
The activation threshold (top 0.5%) and IoU cutoff (0.04) are fixed; sensitivity to these choices is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are correct, and all rows correctly link to none. The only polysemanticity-related text is in the background section: dissection 'can only interpret disentangled neurons', and the rest may detect mixed features. This is a passing explanation, not a result.

versions.untested_parts: Whether individual vision-model neurons respond strongly to several unrelated inputs.
Language-model neurons and unrelated tokens or contexts.
Superposition and capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure and its possible causes.
Changes in polysemantic-neuron share due to activation, architecture, or regularization, including performance costs.
Whether apparent polysemantic neurons actually detect a shared feature or related jobs.
Whether the polysemanticity result changes with activation range or explanation-scoring choices.
